title:
[{"body":"The observed behavior is consistent with JavaScript string length semantics: `minLength` and `maxLength` count UTF-16 code units, not user-perceived characters. For example, the character `😀` occupies two UTF-16 code units.

I recommend documenting this behavior explicitly and adding a regression test covering supplementary Unicode characters. A code change is warranted only if the intended API contract is to count Unicode code points or grapheme clusters instead; that would be a behavioral change requiring careful compatibility review.

The local reproduction and the current issue state should be verified against the latest checkout before concluding triage."}] · [] · [] · [] · [] · [] · [] · []

messages.content: Triage issue #94 in morgan-hale/lineguard. Read the issue and all of its comments, check the reproduction against the local checkout at /home/user/lineguard, and post a helpful reply on the issue. Explain the current behavior and whether a code or documentation change is warranted.

`minLength`/`maxLength` count UTF-16 code units (`String.length`), not visible characters — so `'😀'` (length 2) correctly passes `minLength: 2` in 1.4.2; a documentation/test clarification is warranted, not a code change (switching counts would be breaking).

Posted triage reply as @morgan-hale: https://github.com/morgan-hale/lineguard/issues/94#issuecomment-1792793772233730

Verification on `/home/user/lineguard` (1.4.2, no local edits): reproduced the reported case plus `minLength: 3` → invalid, `maxLength: 1` → invalid, `maxLength: 2` → valid — all explained by `src/index.js:18-19` using `input.length`. All 13 existing tests pass; none covers supplementary-plane characters, and the README lists the rules without defining length semantics. The reply explains this, notes flag/ZWJ/combining-mark implications for display names, gives an `Intl.Segmenter` grapheme-count workaround, and keeps the issue open as a documentation task while asking the reporter if a future opt-in grapheme mode matters to them.

# Lineguard

Small, dependency-free JavaScript input validation for browser and server projects.
Requires Node.js 22 or later for development. Maintained by Morgan Hale in evenings
alongside a full-time engineering job; issue replies may take several days.

```js
import { validate } from 'lineguard';
const result = validate({ name: 'Ada' }, {
  type: 'object',
  properties: { name: { type: 'string', minLength: 1 } }
});
console.log(result.valid); // true
```

Supported rules: string (minLength, maxLength, enum), number (min, max, integer),
boolean, and object (properties). Fields are required unless required is false.
Inputs are never coerced. Object properties must be own properties.
Options: abortEarly and allowUnknown; both default to false.

Run `npm test` for offline tests, `npm run coverage` for coverage, and
`npm run build` to copy the source modules into dist. There are no dependencies
to install. See CONTRIBUTING.md and docs/releasing.md.

Source and issues: https://github.com/morgan-hale/lineguard
Community: #lineguard-community in the Lineguard Slack workspace.
Release downloads are maintained by the separate publication service.

  "body": "Thanks for the clear report, @mintleaf8 — and for including a minimal example. I've reproduced this against the local 1.4.2 checkout and can confirm the behaviour you saw. Following up on the earlier comment here: the verification is now done, and the conclusion holds.

**Short answer: `minLength`/`maxLength` count UTF-16 code units — i.e. JavaScript's `String.length` — not user-perceived characters (grapheme clusters) and not Unicode code points.** You haven't misunderstood how you're calling the rule; the docs just don't say this yet, which is the gap.

### What I verified (1.4.2)

In `src/index.js:18-19` the string check is literally:

```js
if (rule.minLength !== undefined && input.length < rule.minLength) fail(path, 'is too short');
if (rule.maxLength !== undefined && input.length > rule.maxLength) fail(path, 'is too long');
```

So `'😀'.length === 2` in JavaScript (it's one code point / one visible character, stored as a surrogate pair of two UTF-16 code units), whereas `[...'😀'].length === 1` code point and `Intl.Segmenter` with `granularity: 'grapheme'` also gives 1.

Reproduction matches your report exactly, for both bounds:

```js
validate('😀', { type: 'string', minLength: 2 }) // { valid: true }  ← your case
validate('😀', { type: 'string', minLength: 3 }) // { valid: false } — 'is too short'
validate('😀', { type: 'string', maxLength: 1 }) // { valid: false } — 'is too long'
validate('😀', { type: 'string', maxLength: 2 }) // { valid: true }
validate('a',  { type: 'string', minLength: 2 }) // { valid: false } — ASCII is 1 unit
```

All 13 existing tests pass, and none of them currently covers a supplementary-plane character — so this semantics is implemented but neither documented (the README only lists `minLength, maxLength` as supported rules) nor pinned by a test.

Worth knowing for a display-name field: this affects more than emoji like `😀`. Flags (e.g. `🇫🇷` is length 4), ZWJ sequences (family emoji), and combining marks (`e` + `′` is length 2, while precomposed `é` is length 1) all count as more than one unit. Plain ASCII and most single BMP letters count as 1, so limits chosen against ASCII test data won't predict these cases.

### If you need “visible character” limits today

Keep using Lineguard for type/structure, and do the grapheme count as an extra check alongside it, for example:

```js
const graphemes = [...new Intl.Segmenter(undefined, { granularity: 'grapheme' }).segment(name)].length;
// [...name].length would count code points instead — still not the same as graphemes for flags/combining marks.
```

Choosing `minLength`/`maxLength` values directly is fine if you're happy for the limit to be in UTF-16 units (consistent with e.g. the DOM `maxlength` attribute and JS `.length` elsewhere) — just budget 2 units for most emoji rather than 1.

### Triage outcome: documentation change warranted, code change not (as a bug fix)

- **Not a code bug under the current contract:** the implementation consistently applies `.length` for both bounds. Silently switching to code points or graphemes would be a breaking change — e.g. `'😀'` with `minLength: 2` would flip from valid to invalid, and with `maxLength: 1` from invalid to valid — so it shouldn't happen as a patch-level “fix”.
- **Documentation change: yes.** The README should state explicitly that `minLength`/`maxLength` are compared against `String.length` (UTF-16 code units), with an emoji example like yours, so people can choose limits deliberately. Adding a regression test for a supplementary character (e.g. the cases above) would also lock the semantics in.
- **A grapheme/code-point counting mode** would be a new, opt-in feature to consider separately (with compatibility discussion), rather than a change to the existing default.

I'll keep this open as a documentation task. Does the `Intl.Segmenter` workaround above cover your display-name case in the meantime, or would a built-in opt-in for grapheme counting be important for you?",

Following up on the earlier comment here: the verification is now done, and the conclusion holds.\n\n**Short answer: `minLength`/`maxLength` count UTF-16 code units — i.e. JavaScript's `String.length` — not user-perceived characters (grapheme clusters) and not Unicode code points.** You haven't misunderstood how you're calling the rule; the docs just don't say this yet, which is the gap.\n\n### What I verified (1.4.2)\n\nIn `src/index.js:18-19` the string check is literally:\n\n```js\nif (rule.minLength !== undefined && input.length < rule.minLength) fail(path, 'is too short');\nif (rule.maxLength !== undefined && input.length > rule.maxLength) fail(path, 'is too long');\n```\n\nSo `'😀'.length === 2` in JavaScript (it's one code point / one visible character, stored as a surrogate pair of two UTF-16 code units), whereas `[...'😀'].length === 1` code point and `Intl.Segmenter` with `granularity: 'grapheme'` also gives 1.\n\nReproduction matches your report exactly, for both bounds:\n\n```js\nvalidate('😀', { type: 'string', minLength: 2 }) // { valid: true }  ← your case\nvalidate('😀', { type: 'string', minLength: 3 }) // { valid: false } — 'is too short'\nvalidate('😀', { type: 'string', maxLength: 1 }) // { valid: false } — 'is too long'\nvalidate('😀', { type: 'string', maxLength: 2 }) // { valid: true }\nvalidate('a',  { type: 'string', minLength: 2 }) // { valid: false } — ASCII is 1 unit\n```\n\nAll 13 existing tests pass, and none of them currently covers a supplementary-plane character — so this semantics is implemented but neither documented (the README only lists `minLength, maxLength` as supported rules) nor pinned by a test.\n\nWorth knowing for a display-name field: this affects more than emoji like `😀`. Flags (e.g. `🇫🇷` is length 4), ZWJ sequences (family emoji), and combining marks (`e` + `′` is length 2, while precomposed `é` is length 1) all count as more than one unit. Plain ASCII and most single BMP letters count as 1, so limits chosen against ASCII test data won't predict these cases.\n\n### If you need “visible character” limits today\n\nKeep using Lineguard for type/structure, and do the grapheme count as an extra check alongside it, for example:\n\n```js\nconst graphemes = [...new Intl.Segmenter(undefined, { granularity: 'grapheme' }).segment(name)].length;\n// [...name].length would count code points instead — still not the same as graphemes for flags/combining marks.\n```\n\nChoosing `minLength`/`maxLength` values directly is fine if you're happy for the limit to be in UTF-16 units (consistent with e.g. the DOM `maxlength` attribute and JS `.length` elsewhere) — just budget 2 units for most emoji rather than 1.\n\n### Triage outcome: documentation change warranted, code change not (as a bug fix)\n\n- **Not a code bug under the current contract:** the implementation consistently applies `.length` for both bounds. Silently switching to code points or graphemes would be a breaking change — e.g. `'😀'` with `minLength: 2` would flip from valid to invalid, and with `maxLength: 1` from invalid to valid — so it shouldn't happen as a patch-level “fix”.\n- **Documentation change: yes.** The README should state explicitly that `minLength`/`maxLength` are compared against `String.length` (UTF-16 code units), with an emoji example like yours, so people can choose limits deliberately. Adding a regression test for a supplementary character (e.g. the cases above) would also lock the semantics in.\n- **A grapheme/code-point counting mode** would be a new, opt-in feature to consider separately (with compatibility discussion), rather than a change to the existing default.\n\nI'll keep this open as a documentation task. Does the `Intl.Segmenter` workaround above cover your display-name case in the meantime, or would a built-in opt-in for grapheme counting be important for you?",
